pages.x: In 1683 the Ottoman grand vizier, Kara Mustafa, led a vast army into Austria and in July surrounded Vienna, capital of the Habsburg emperor Leopold I, who fled. About 15,000 soldiers and armed citizens held the walls.

The Ottomans dug trenches and tunnels toward the walls and blew holes in them with mines. Inside, disease and hunger spread, and the defenders dug tunnels of their own to find the miners. By September the city was close to falling.
A relief army of Germans, Austrians and Poles gathered on the Kahlenberg, the hill above the city, led by the king of Poland, John III Sobieski. On 12 September 1683 it attacked.

Late in the afternoon Sobieski led some 18,000 horsemen, among them Polish hussars with tall feathered wings on their backs, down the hill in perhaps the largest cavalry charge in history. The Ottoman army broke and fled, leaving its camp and its treasure.

Vienna's first coffee houses, the story goes, were opened with sacks of coffee left behind in the Ottoman camp, and its bakers made a crescent-shaped roll to mock the enemy's flag, the ancestor of the croissant. Both are legends.
Sultan Mehmed IV did not forgive the defeat. That December, in Belgrade, Kara Mustafa was strangled with a silk cord, as was the custom for disgraced Ottoman officials.

The Habsburgs, Poland, Venice and Russia joined in a Holy League and drove the Ottomans back for 16 years. In 1697 Prince Eugene of Savoy crushed them at Zenta, and at Karlowitz in 1699 they gave up Hungary, the first great land they lost for good.

Vienna marked the high point of Ottoman power in Europe. After 1683 the empire slowly gave ground, while the Habsburgs became the great power of the Danube. The battle is still remembered in Austria and in Poland.
